content: Some adolescent boys reported that the use of device-based voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) disrupted their daily routines and activities. They experienced difficulties in sitting, walking, sleeping, performing household tasks, participating in sports, and attending school. Other factors that were considered important outcomes included healing time, odor, and pain. Healing after male circumcision using the elastic collar compression device occurs by secondary intention, which means it takes longer compared to surgical methods. Healing with this device required at least one additional week compared to surgical circumcision. Consequently, a longer period of sexual abstinence was necessary during the healing process compared to standard surgical methods. Among 1,423 clients, the overall proportion of those fully healed six weeks after circumcision with the elastic collar compression device was 69%, based on data from 3,238 clients. Odor was frequently reported as a barrier to the acceptability of the device. Approximately 58% of clients (1,844 out of 3,173) reported experiencing an unpleasant smell while wearing the device, which was described as a bad odor either during the healing process or upon device removal. A small percentage of clients (4%) stated that they would have opted not to undergo circumcision at all due to this issue. Pain scores were challenging to compare across studies due to variations in pain control protocols. However, the elastic collar compression device did not require injectable anesthesia during placement, unlike conventional surgical circumcision. Studies showed that pain scores were generally higher for surgical circumcision, primarily due to the pain associated with injectable anesthesia. In contrast, topical anesthesia was used with the device in most studies. Pain during device placement and erections was reported to be low, but pain during device removal was higher and more variable across studies. Some clients experienced significant pain during removal, which was managed differently at various study sites, with methods such as lidocaine spray or EMLA cream. The time required for device placement and removal varied depending on the experience of the clinician, with more experienced providers reporting shorter procedure times. Pain scores during device placement were consistently low, but greater pain was reported during device removal. Adolescent boys expressed preferences for different circumcision methods, with some favoring device-based methods over surgical ones. However, barriers to the uptake of device-based VMMC included concerns about pain, longer healing times, and time off from work or school. Health care workers, including physicians and nurses, generally found device-based circumcision methods to be easier to perform, faster, and associated with fewer complications compared to surgical methods. They also noted better cosmetic outcomes and less bleeding with device-based techniques. The cost of device-based circumcision reflected shorter procedure times and reduced clinician involvement compared to surgical methods. However, the additional costs of the device itself, associated medical supplies, and follow-up visits for device removal increased the overall cost. Despite this, many health care workers preferred device-based methods due to their simplicity and efficiency. Healing times for device-based methods were one to two weeks longer than for surgical circumcision, requiring a longer period of sexual abstinence to reduce the risk of HIV acquisition during the healing process. Some adverse events, such as device displacement or slippage, required immediate surgical intervention to prevent serious outcomes. The risk of tetanus with the elastic collar compression device necessitated vaccination prior to the procedure, which could reduce the uptake of VMMC. Cosmetic outcomes were assessed four weeks after the procedure, with 92% of clients achieving a regular appearance. Irregular or scalloped appearances were attributed to the need for suturing in some early cases. Overall, device-based VMMC was found to be acceptable among adolescent and adult males, but specific considerations and challenges were associated with each device type.
